title: Maximize the Beauty of the Garden
statement:
A row of flowers is given as `flowers`, where `flowers[i]` is the beauty of the `i`-th flower (it may be negative or zero). You may remove any number of flowers, including none; the flowers left keep their original order. The remaining garden is *valid* when it has at least two flowers and its first and last flowers have equal beauty. A garden's beauty is the sum of the beauties of the flowers in it.

Return the largest beauty a valid garden can have after your removals. At least one value appears twice in `flowers`, so a valid garden can always be made.
constraints: Some value occurs at least twice in flowers, so a valid garden always exists
notes:
## Intuition

Once you decide which two equal flowers, at positions `i < j`, become the ends of the garden, the rest is easy: keep every positive flower between them and remove everything else. Trying every equal pair and summing the middle is O(n²) or worse. Two observations make it linear:

- A running sum of only the positive beauties (`prefix`) gives the kept middle sum as a difference of two prefix values.
- For a fixed right end, the leftmost earlier flower with the same value is always the best left end, because `prefix` never decreases, so starting earlier can only add more positive flowers.

So a hash map only needs to remember, for each value, the prefix right after its first occurrence.

## Approach

1. Walk through `flowers` keeping `prefix`, the sum of positive beauties seen so far.
2. If `flower` was seen before, the garden from its first occurrence to here has beauty `2 * flower + prefix - firstPrefix.get(flower)`; update `best`.
3. Add `max(flower, 0)` to `prefix`.
4. If this is the value's first occurrence, store the current `prefix` in `firstPrefix`.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`flowers = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2]`.

- `1`: new; `prefix = 1`, store 1 → 1.
- `2`: new; `prefix = 3`, store 2 → 3.
- `3`: new; `prefix = 6`, store 3 → 6.
- `1`: seen; beauty `2 + 6 - 1 = 7` (garden `[1, 2, 3, 1]`), `best = 7`; `prefix = 7`.
- `2`: seen; beauty `4 + 7 - 3 = 8` (garden `[2, 3, 1, 2]`), `best = 8`.

The answer is `8`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant-time map operations.
- Space: O(n) for the map of distinct values.

## Pitfalls

- The two end flowers count even when negative; only the middle flowers are optional.
- Store the prefix *after* adding the first occurrence, so that flower is not counted twice.
- Keep only the first occurrence of each value; overwriting it with later ones loses better gardens.
- Start `best` at `-Infinity` (or a huge negative), since the answer can be negative.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `firstPrefix` | value → `prefix` just after that value's first occurrence |
| `prefix` | sum of the positive beauties seen so far |
| `best` | largest valid garden beauty found |
| `flower` | the current flower's beauty |
| `beauty` | beauty of the garden ending at the current flower |

narration.2: For each value, remember the positive prefix sum just after its first occurrence.
narration.3: Running sum of the positive beauties only, since those are the middle flowers worth keeping.
narration.4: The answer may be negative, so start below every possible beauty.
narration.6: Treat each flower in turn as the last flower of the garden.
narration.7: A valid garden needs an earlier flower with the same beauty.
narration.8: Both end flowers plus every positive flower strictly between the first occurrence and here.
narration.9: Keep the best garden seen so far.
narration.11: Grow the positive prefix with this flower if it helps.
narration.12: Only the first occurrence of a value is the best left end.
narration.13: Store the prefix after this flower so it is not counted again as a middle flower.
narration.16: Return the most beautiful valid garden.
